QF.id: Clubbing, Set-Off and Carry Forward of Losses_2

question.text: Rekha has a 25% share in the profits of M/s Dhanush Enterprises, a partnership firm. Her husband Mohan is employed by the same firm and receives a salary of Rs.6,00,000 per year. Mohan does not hold any professional qualifications relevant to his role. In whose hands will Mohan's salary be clubbed?

answer.text: Mohan's income, since salary is always taxable in the hands of the person earning it
Shared equally between Rekha and Mohan
The partnership firm's income, as it is a disallowed expense
Rekha's income, as she has substantial interest in the concern employing Mohan and he lacks relevant professional qualifications

explanation.text: The Logic: Under the clubbing provisions of the Income-tax Act, where an individual has a substantial interest in a concern, any remuneration paid by that concern to the individual's spouse is generally clubbed with the income of the individual who has the substantial interest. An exception applies where the spouse possesses technical or professional qualifications and the remuneration is attributable solely to the application of those qualifications. In this scenario, Rekha holds a 25% share in the firm's profits, giving her a substantial interest in the firm, and Mohan does not hold any relevant professional qualifications, so the professional-qualification exception does not apply. Mohan's salary is therefore clubbed with Rekha's income. The Trap: Salary is not always taxable only in the hands of the person earning it; the clubbing provisions can override that default in specified family-and-business situations. Equal sharing between spouses is not how the clubbing rule operates. Treating the salary as a disallowed expense of the firm confuses business-deduction rules with personal-income clubbing. Note: The cited workbook chapter discusses clubbing of income generally, including spouse-related clubbing, but does not spell out the specific Section 64(1)(ii) "substantial interest" employment rule, a quantified threshold for substantial interest, or the professional-qualification exception. The framing above reflects the general Income-tax Act / clubbing-of-income rules rather than a direct workbook citation.
